claims.text: The initial Al–Mg–Ti–Zn alloy is a metastable, predominantly FCC solid solution.
The initial alloy contains approximately 15–25 at.% Mg.
The initial alloy has minimal intermetallic precipitation.
Local Mg diffusion in the metastable matrix drives heterogeneous nucleation and growth of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-containing alloys in the relevant compositional family tend to form Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The Mg-rich precipitates nucleate preferentially at grain boundaries and Ti-enriched regions.
Short annealing produces a fine, uniformly distributed network of nanoscale intermetallic precipitates.
A fine and uniform intermetallic distribution promotes formation of a protective passive surface film and high corrosion resistance.
The precipitate-mediated passive film is coherent and TiO2-rich.
Mg-rich precipitates act as sites for subsequent TiO2 formation.
Prolonged annealing or accelerated transformation kinetics cause substantial coarsening of the Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Excessive precipitate coarsening disrupts the integrity and coherence of the passive oxide layer.
Short annealing will retain or improve corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast metastable state.
Short annealing will retain or improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
Prolonged annealing will degrade corrosion resistance, including increasing corrosion current density.
Prolonged annealing will degrade high-temperature oxidation behavior.
Replacing part of the Mg with Sc suppresses Mg diffusion while preserving sufficiently similar phase equilibria and baseline corrosion behavior.
The Sc-substituted control will exhibit suppressed intermetallic evolution and retain the metastable state during annealing.
Approximately 300 °C represents the lower-temperature corrosion-service regime, whereas approximately 600 °C represents the high-temperature oxidative-service regime.
Similar precipitation, passive-film evolution, and resistance changes in the baseline and Mg-diffusion-suppressed control would falsify the proposed Mg-driven mechanism.
